claim: Wave command-like neurons in Drosophila larvae diversify their wiring and function in a segment-specific manner.
source: We address this question in Drosophila larvae by focusing on segmentally homologous Wave command-like neurons, which diversify their wiring and function in a segment-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Anterior Wave (a-Wave) neurons extend axons anteriorly and connect to circuits inducing backward locomotion.
source: Anterior Wave (a-Wave) neurons extend axons anteriorly and connect to circuits inducing backward locomotion, whereas posterior Wave (p-Wave) neurons extend axons posteriorly and trigger forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work (Takagi et al., 2017).

claim: Posterior Wave (p-Wave) neurons extend axons posteriorly and trigger forward locomotion.
source: Anterior Wave (a-Wave) neurons extend axons anteriorly and connect to circuits inducing backward locomotion, whereas posterior Wave (p-Wave) neurons extend axons posteriorly and trigger forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work (Takagi et al., 2017).

claim: Frizzled receptors DFz2 and DFz4, together with the DWnt4 ligand, regulate the segment-specific Wave axon projection.
source: Here, we show that Frizzled receptors DFz2 and DFz4, together with the DWnt4 ligand, regulate the segment-specific Wave axon projection.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: DFz2 knockdown reroutes Wave axons to posterior neuromeres.
source: DFz2 knockdown (KD) not only reroutes Wave axons to posterior neuromeres but also biases its motor command to induce forward instead of backward locomotion as tactile response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 1 and 7.

claim: DFz2 knockdown biases Wave motor command to induce forward instead of backward locomotion as tactile response.
source: DFz2 knockdown (KD) not only reroutes Wave axons to posterior neuromeres but also biases its motor command to induce forward instead of backward locomotion as tactile response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Segment-specific axon guidance diversifies the function of homologous command neurons in behavioral regulation.
source: Thus, segment-specific axon guidance diversifies the function of homologous command neurons in behavioral regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Control of anterior-posterior (A-P) axon guidance by Wnt/Fz signaling is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Since control of anterior-posterior (A-P) axon guidance by Wnt/Fz signaling is evolutionarily conserved, our results reveal a potentially universal molecular principle for formation and diversification of the command system in the nerve cord.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work in mammals and C. elegans (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Lyuksyutova et al., 2003).

claim: Sensorimotor transduction can be rerouted by manipulating a single gene in a single class of neurons.
source: Furthermore, this work indicates that sensorimotor transduction can be rerouted by manipulating a single gene in a single class of neurons, potentially facilitating the evolutionary flexibility in action selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DFz2 knockdown experiments showing behavioral changes.

claim: Wave neurons are present in identical positions in each abdominal neuromere, A1-A7.
source: Wave neurons are present in identical positions in each abdominal neuromere, A1-A7, and extend their proximal axons to the neuropile in similar manners (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wave neurons extend their proximal axons to the neuropile in similar manners.
source: Wave neurons are present in identical positions in each abdominal neuromere, A1-A7, and extend their proximal axons to the neuropile in similar manners (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wave neurons in anterior segments (a-Wave; in neuromeres A1-A3) extend axons anteriorly.
source: Wave neurons in anterior segments (a-Wave; in neuromeres A1-A3) extend axons anteriorly and connect to circuits inducing backward locomotion, whereas Wave neurons in posterior segments (p-Wave; in neuromeres A4-A7) extend axons posteriorly and elicit forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Wave neurons in posterior segments (p-Wave; in neuromeres A4-A7) extend axons posteriorly.
source: Wave neurons in anterior segments (a-Wave; in neuromeres A1-A3) extend axons anteriorly and connect to circuits inducing backward locomotion, whereas Wave neurons in posterior segments (p-Wave; in neuromeres A4-A7) extend axons posteriorly and elicit forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and shown in Figure 1.

claim: DFz2 is necessary for the suppression of Wave neurite outgrowth toward the posterior end.
source: In summary, DFz2 is necessary for the suppression of Wave neurite outgrowth toward the posterior end (Figure 1M), and such suppression might be indispensable to diversify Wave neuron connectivity across segments.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the DFz2 knockdown and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The abnormal extension of Wave axons toward the posterior end upon DFz2 KD was accompanied by presynaptic varicosities en route.
source: Notably, the abnormal extension of Wave axons toward the posterior end was accompanied by presynaptic varicosities en route (Figure 1D and E), suggesting that ectopic synapses are formed in this region.
evidence: This is an observation from the single-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Ectopic synapses are formed in the region of abnormal Wave axon extension upon DFz2 KD.
source: Notably, the abnormal extension of Wave axons toward the posterior end was accompanied by presynaptic varicosities en route (Figure 1D and E), suggesting that ectopic synapses are formed in this region.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of presynaptic varicosities and confirmed by Bruchpilot staining in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of DFz2 in Wave neurons results in the shortening of a-Wave axon extension toward the posterior end.
source: Conversely, overexpression of DFz2 in Wave neurons resulted in the shortening of a-Wave (but not p-Wave) axon extension toward the posterior end (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: DFz2 overexpression does not affect p-Wave axon extension toward the posterior end.
source: Conversely, overexpression of DFz2 in Wave neurons resulted in the shortening of a-Wave (but not p-Wave) axon extension toward the posterior end (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1L.

claim: DFz2 KD results in posterior extension of the dendrites of Wave neurons.
source: Aside from axons, we also found a posterior extension of the dendrites of Wave neurons in DFz2 KD animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ectopic extension of dendrites in DFz2 KD animals was much shorter and occurred less frequently as compared to that of the axon.
source: However, the ectopic extension of dendrites was much shorter and occurred less frequently as compared to that of the axon.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The conserved dendritic extension pattern suggests that a-Wave neurons still receive inputs from tactile sensory neurons in anterior segments in DFz2 KD animals as in the wild type.
source: The conserved dendritic extension pattern suggests that a-Wave neurons still receive inputs from tactile sensory neurons in anterior segments in DFz2 KD animals as in the wild type (Takagi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the dendritic morphology and previous work (Takagi et al., 2017).

claim: The outputs of Wave neurons are more likely to be rerouted by DFz2 KD in a-Wave neurons than the inputs.
source: Thus, while it cannot be completely excluded that there are some changes in the inputs, the outputs are more likely to be rerouted by DFz2 KD in a-Wave neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that axonal changes are more pronounced than dendritic changes.

claim: Synapses are formed at all the neuromeres where the A4-Wave axon is projecting.
source: While not all the boutons were Brp+ (Figure 2A and B), we observed that synapses are formed at all the neuromere where the A4-Wave axon is projecting (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The number of synapses was shifted toward posterior neuromeres upon DFz2 KD.
source: Importantly, the number of synapses was shifted toward posterior neuromeres upon DFz2 KD, which is a pattern similar to the axon projection phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The fraction of synapses over all boutons was relatively uniform across neuromeres.
source: The fraction of synapses over all boutons was relatively uniform across neuromeres (Figure 2E), indicating that presynaptic varicosities are a decent indicator of synapses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Presynaptic varicosities are a decent indicator of synapses.
source: The fraction of synapses over all boutons was relatively uniform across neuromeres (Figure 2E), indicating that presynaptic varicosities are a decent indicator of synapses.
evidence: This is inferred from the uniform fraction of synapses over boutons shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DFz2 KD results in ectopic downstream Wave connectivity, possibly altering the motor command upon its activation.
source: These observations suggest that DFz2 KD results in ectopic downstream Wave connectivity, possibly altering the motor command upon its activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the synapse distribution data in Figure 2.

claim: Posterior axon extension of the most posterior p-Wave neuron (A6-Wave) is shortened in DFz4 KD animals.
source: We also found that posterior axon extension of the most posterior p-Wave neuron (A6-Wave) is shortened in DFz4 KD animals (Figure 3A–I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: DFz4 mediates attraction of the p-Wave axons toward the posterior end.
source: This observation suggests that DFz4 mediates attraction of the p-Wave axons toward the posterior end.
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz4 KD phenotype shown in Figure 3.

claim: DFz4 promotes axon extension of Wave axons selectively in A6-Wave and toward the posterior end.
source: Neither posterior extension of other Wave axons (Figure 3C–F) nor the anterior extension of A6 or other Wave axons (Figure 3C–G) was affected, implying that DFz4 promotes axon extension of Wave axons selectively in A6-Wave and toward the posterior end (summarized in Figure 3J).
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the DFz4 KD phenotype shown in Figure 3.

claim: DFz4 overexpression did not yield any obvious morphological changes.
source: DFz4 overexpression did not yield any obvious morphological changes (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that DFz4 expression alone is not sufficient to change the axon extension of Wave neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: DFz4 expression alone is not sufficient to change the axon extension of Wave neurons.
source: DFz4 overexpression did not yield any obvious morphological changes (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that DFz4 expression alone is not sufficient to change the axon extension of Wave neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype upon DFz4 overexpression shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: p-Wave axon extension toward the posterior end was shortened in DWnt4 mutants.
source: We first examined the overall extension pattern of Wave neurites in four Drosophila Wnt mutants (DWnt4C1/EMS23, DWnt5400, DWnt6KO, and DWnt8KO1) and found that p-Wave axon extension toward the posterior end was shortened in DWnt4 mutants, which is reminiscent of DFz4 KD animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and Figure 4A–C.

claim: DWnt4 is known to have binding affinity to both DFz2 and DFz4.
source: DWnt4 is known to have binding affinity to both DFz2 and DFz4 (Wu and Nusse, 2002), making it a strong candidate as a shared ligand of these receptors in Wave axon guidance.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Wu and Nusse, 2002).

claim: Posterior extension of a-Wave axons was elongated in DWnt4 mutants.
source: Further analyses with single-Wave labeling (by using heat-shock FlpOut) also revealed abnormalities in a-Wave; posterior extension of a-Wave axons was elongated, as was observed in DFz2 KD animals (Figure 4D, E, and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D, E, and G.

claim: a-Wave axon extension toward the anterior end was shortened in DWnt4 mutants.
source: Additionally, a-Wave axon extension toward the anterior end was shortened in DWnt4 mutants (Figure 4D, E, and F), which was not observed in DFz2 or DFz4 receptor KD animals, suggesting that DWnt4 regulates anterior extension of a-Wave via other receptor(s).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D, E, and F.

claim: DWnt4 regulates anterior extension of a-Wave via other receptor(s) besides DFz2 and DFz4.
source: Additionally, a-Wave axon extension toward the anterior end was shortened in DWnt4 mutants (Figure 4D, E, and F), which was not observed in DFz2 or DFz4 receptor KD animals, suggesting that DWnt4 regulates anterior extension of a-Wave via other receptor(s).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of DWnt4 mutant and DFz2/DFz4 KD phenotypes.

claim: Both DFz2 and DFz4 use DWnt4 as a guidance cue to regulate the extension of Wave axons along the A-P axis but with opposite 'valences'.
source: The fact that DWnt4 mutants recapitulated both phenotypes observed in DFz2 and DFz4 KD animals (Figure 4H) suggests that both DFz2 and DFz4 use DWnt4 as a guidance cue to regulate the extension of Wave axons along the A-P axis but with opposite 'valences'.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of DWnt4 mutant and DFz2/DFz4 KD phenotypes shown in Figure 4H.

claim: DWnt4 mRNAs are strongly expressed at the posterior end of the VNC.
source: It has been previously suggested that DWnt4 mRNAs are strongly expressed at the posterior end of the VNC (Hessinger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Hessinger et al., 2017).

claim: The expression of DWnt4 shows a gradient with higher expression toward the posterior end of the VNC.
source: Our analyses of DWnt4 knock-in GAL4 line (Wnt4MI03717-Trojan-GAL4) further confirmed that the expression of DWnt4 shows a gradient with higher expression toward the posterior end of the VNC (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DWnt4 protein expression shows a gradient within the neuropil with higher expression toward the posterior end.
source: Furthermore, DWnt4 immunostaining revealed a similar gradient within the neuropil (Figure 5C and D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B), indicating that protein expression is also polarized.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: DWnt4 regulates axon guidance along the A-P axis by forming a gradient along the axis.
source: These observations support the notion that DWnt4 regulates axon guidance along the A-P axis by forming a gradient along the axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the gradient expression of DWnt4 shown in Figure 5.

claim: DFz2 expression shows a weak bidirectional gradient along the A-P axis, with a slightly higher level of expression in the anterior part of the VNC neuropil.
source: We observed a weak bidirectional gradient of DFz2 expression along the A-P axis, with a slightly higher level of expression in the anterior part of the VNC neuropil (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D), as well as in the posterior end (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and F and Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Complementary expression of DWnt4 and DFz2 regulates Wave axon extension via repulsion.
source: Collectively, these results are consistent with the idea that complementary expression of DWnt4 and DFz2 regulates Wave axon extension via repulsion: Wave axons with higher levels of DFz2 and thus with higher sensitivity to repulsive DWnt4 signaling extend to the anterior VNC where levels of DWnt4 are low (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns of DWnt4 and DFz2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: DFz4 guides p-Wave axons posteriorly by recognizing DWnt4 as an attractive cue.
source: Nonetheless, based on the phenotype of DFz4 KD (Figure 3) and the expression of DWnt4, it is likely that DFz4 guides p-Wave axons posteriorly by recognizing DWnt4 as an attractive cue (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz4 KD phenotype and DWnt4 expression pattern.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of all Wave neurons in the larvae induces a mixture of fast-forward locomotion, backward locomotion, and roll/bend.
source: Consistent with this, optogenetic stimulation of all Wave neurons in the larvae induces a mixture of fast-forward locomotion, backward locomotion, and roll/bend (Takagi et al., 2017; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Takagi et al., 2017) and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In control animals, optogenetic stimulation of Wave neurons induced fast-forward locomotion, backward locomotion, and rolling.
source: In control animals, as observed previously (Takagi et al., 2017), the stimulation induced fast-forward locomotion (Figure 6B), backward locomotion (Figure 6B'), and rolling (Figure 6B'').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B, B', and B''.

claim: In DFz2 KD animals, optogenetic stimulation of Wave neurons induced fast-forward locomotion and rolling but not backward locomotion.
source: By contrast, in DFz2 KD animals, the stimulation induced fast-forward locomotion (Figure 6C) and rolling (Figure 6C'') but not backward locomotion (Figure 6C').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C, C', and C''.

claim: The speed of the evoked fast-forward locomotion (during stimulation) was faster in DFz2 KD animals, while the baseline speed was unchanged.
source: Importantly, we found that the speed of the evoked fast-forward locomotion (during stimulation) was faster in DFz2 KD animals, while the baseline speed was unchanged (Figure 6D and E), indicating that fast-forward locomotion is enhanced in DFz2 KD animals upon Wave activation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Fast-forward locomotion is enhanced in DFz2 KD animals upon Wave activation.
source: Importantly, we found that the speed of the evoked fast-forward locomotion (during stimulation) was faster in DFz2 KD animals, while the baseline speed was unchanged (Figure 6D and E), indicating that fast-forward locomotion is enhanced in DFz2 KD animals upon Wave activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the stride duration data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: DFz2 KD in Wave neurons augments their motor command of fast-forward locomotion while diminishing that of backward locomotion.
source: In summary, DFz2 KD in Wave neurons augments their motor command of fast-forward locomotion while diminishing that of backward locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: DFz2 KD by using two different RNAi lines in Wave neurons reduced backward locomotion responses (scores 3 and 4) while increasing turning responses (score 2) to head touch.
source: We found that DFz2 KD by using two different RNAi lines in Wave neurons reduced backward locomotion responses (scores 3 and 4) while increasing turning responses (score 2) to head touch (Figure 7B, B', C, and C').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B, B', C, and C'.

claim: The speed of forward locomotion after each touch (usually after turning) was faster in DFz2 KD animals.
source: Critically, the speed of forward locomotion after each touch (usually after turning) was faster in DFz2 KD animals (Figure 7B'' and C''), implying that fast-forward locomotion was induced in response to tactile stimulus.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B'' and C''.

claim: Fast-forward locomotion was induced in response to tactile stimulus in DFz2 KD animals.
source: Critically, the speed of forward locomotion after each touch (usually after turning) was faster in DFz2 KD animals (Figure 7B'' and C''), implying that fast-forward locomotion was induced in response to tactile stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the faster forward locomotion speed shown in Figure 7B'' and C''.

claim: Changes in the axon guidance of Wave neurons alter the behavioral strategy of the larvae in response to external stimuli by altering the neurons' command from backward to fast-forward locomotion.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that changes in the axon guidance of Wave neurons alter the behavioral strategy of the larvae in response to external stimuli by altering the neurons' command from backward to fast-forward locomotion (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Wnt/Fz signaling regulates A-P axon pathfinding in the nervous system of mammals and Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Wnt/Fz signaling is known to regulate A-P axon pathfinding in the nervous system of mammals and Caenorhabditis elegans (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Lyuksyutova et al., 2003; Salinas and Zou, 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006; Lyuksyutova et al., 2003; Salinas and Zou, 2008).

claim: Commissural neurons in the mouse spinal cord after crossing the midline extend their axons anteriorly by recognizing an anterior-high gradient of Wnt4 via the Frizzled-3 receptor.
source: For instance, commissural neurons in the mouse spinal cord after crossing the midline extend their axons anteriorly by recognizing an anterior-high gradient of Wnt4 via the Frizzled-3 receptor (Lyuksyutova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Lyuksyutova et al., 2003).

claim: lin-44/Wnt and lin-17/Frizzled regulate the A-P extension of the PLM mechanosensory neuron in C. elegans.
source: Similarly, lin-44/Wnt and lin-17/Frizzled regulate the A-P extension of the PLM mechanosensory neuron in C. elegans (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Hilliard and Bargmann, 2006).

claim: Wnt/Fz proteins regulate axon guidance in Drosophila.
source: Although Wnt/Fz proteins are known to regulate axon guidance in Drosophila (e.g. Inaki et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2006; Yoshikawa et al., 2003), whether they play roles in A-P neurite guidance in the nerve cord was not previously known.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Inaki et al., 2007; Sato et al., 2006; Yoshikawa et al., 2003).

claim: The present study demonstrates that Wnt/Fz signaling plays roles in A-P neurite guidance in the Drosophila nerve cord.
source: The present study demonstrates this in Drosophila and thus points to the universal roles played by Wnt/Fz signaling in A-P neurite guidance in the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt/Fz signaling plays universal roles in A-P neurite guidance in the animal kingdom.
source: The present study demonstrates this in Drosophila and thus points to the universal roles played by Wnt/Fz signaling in A-P neurite guidance in the animal kingdom.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of Wnt/Fz signaling in A-P axon guidance across species.

claim: DFz4 mediates attraction of posterior Wave neurons toward the source of DWnt4 at the posterior end.
source: Our results suggest that DFz4 mediates attraction of posterior Wave neurons toward the source of DWnt4 at the posterior end, whereas DFz2 mediates repulsion of both anterior and posterior Wave neurons away from the DWnt4 source.
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz4 KD phenotype and DWnt4 expression pattern.

claim: DFz2 mediates repulsion of both anterior and posterior Wave neurons away from the DWnt4 source.
source: Our results suggest that DFz4 mediates attraction of posterior Wave neurons toward the source of DWnt4 at the posterior end, whereas DFz2 mediates repulsion of both anterior and posterior Wave neurons away from the DWnt4 source.
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz2 KD phenotype and DWnt4 expression pattern.

claim: The presence of two graded signaling systems with antagonistic effects may aid in establishing reliable A-P axon guidance.
source: The presence of two graded signaling systems with antagonistic effects may aid in establishing reliable A-P axon guidance as proposed by theoretical models (Gierer, 1987).
evidence: This is stated based on theoretical models (Gierer, 1987).

claim: The two signaling systems (DFz2 and DFz4) cooperate to guide the projection of Wave axons along the A-P axis.
source: Our functional analyses of DFz2 and DFz4 receptors support the idea that the two signaling systems cooperate to guide the projection of Wave axons along the A-P axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional analyses of DFz2 and DFz4 presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt/Fz signaling likely regulates A-P guidance of many other longitudinal axons, since DFz2 immunoreactivity was seen on a large fraction of axons in the anterior VNC.
source: While this study focused on Wave neurons, it is likely that Wnt/Fz signaling also regulates A-P guidance of many other longitudinal axons, since DFz2 immunoreactivity was seen on a large fraction of axons in the anterior VNC.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread DFz2 expression shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Modulation of input connectivity to command neurons is known to alter sensory-evoked behaviors.
source: Indeed, modulation of input connectivity to command neurons is known to alter sensory-evoked behaviors (Tenedini et al., 2019; Valdes-Aleman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Tenedini et al., 2019; Valdes-Aleman et al., 2021).

claim: DFz2 KD appears to influence both the axon projection pattern of a-Wave neurons and their associated motor outputs, shifting the behavioral response from backward to forward locomotion.
source: Here, we found that DFz2 KD appears to influence both the axon projection pattern of a-Wave neurons and their associated motor outputs, shifting the behavioral response from backward to forward locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic and behavioral experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The specificity of Wave-mediated motor commands plays important roles in shaping larval behavior.
source: These findings imply that the specificity of Wave-mediated motor commands plays important roles in shaping larval behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral changes observed upon DFz2 KD in Wave neurons.

claim: Posterior axon projection and connection with forward-inducing circuits are a default state of Wave neurons.
source: The fact that DFz2 KD a-Wave neurons function like p-Wave neurons and induce forward locomotion suggests that posterior axon projection and connection with forward-inducing circuits are a default state of Wave neurons and that suppression of posterior extension by Wnt/DFz2 is required for a-Wave to connect to alternative downstream circuits (those inducing backward locomotion) and acquire an alternative motor command.
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz2 KD phenotype where a-Wave neurons behave like p-Wave neurons.

claim: Suppression of posterior extension by Wnt/DFz2 is required for a-Wave to connect to alternative downstream circuits (those inducing backward locomotion) and acquire an alternative motor command.
source: The fact that DFz2 KD a-Wave neurons function like p-Wave neurons and induce forward locomotion suggests that posterior axon projection and connection with forward-inducing circuits are a default state of Wave neurons and that suppression of posterior extension by Wnt/DFz2 is required for a-Wave to connect to alternative downstream circuits (those inducing backward locomotion) and acquire an alternative motor command.
evidence: This is inferred from the DFz2 KD phenotype where a-Wave neurons behave like p-Wave neurons.

claim: Command functions of segmentally homologous neurons may diverge during development by Wnt/DFz2-mediated suppression of posterior axon extension.
source: Our findings suggest a possible mechanism by which command functions of segmentally homologous neurons may diverge during development, potentially contributing to diverse sensory-motor transformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Simply guiding the axon to a novel position appears to be sufficient for synapse formation with alternative downstream circuits.
source: First, simply guiding the axon to a novel position appears to be sufficient for synapse formation with alternative downstream circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that a-Wave neurons in DFz2 KD animals form synapses in ectopic locations and acquire forward-inducing ability.

claim: a-Wave neurons in DFz2 KD animals likely formed synapses with neural circuits that trigger fast-forward locomotion, presumably the downstream targets of p-Wave.
source: Since a-Wave neurons acquired the ability to induce fast-forward locomotion in DFz2 KD animals, these neurons likely formed synapses with neural circuits that trigger the behavior, presumably the downstream targets of p-Wave.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral changes observed upon DFz2 KD in a-Wave neurons.

claim: Neurons have robust capacity to form synapses with nontarget cells, for instance, when placed in an ectopic position or when normal targets are deleted.
source: It is known that neurons have robust capacity to form synapses with nontarget cells, for instance, when placed in an ectopic position or when normal targets are deleted (Bekkers and Stevens, 1991; Cash et al., 1992; Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Bekkers and Stevens, 1991; Cash et al., 1992; Hassan and Hiesinger, 2015; Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Xu et al., 2019).

claim: a-Wave and p-Wave neurons are segmental homologs and likely share a large fraction of gene expression including those involved in synapse formation.
source: Furthermore, since a-Wave and p-Wave neurons are segmental homologs and likely share a large fraction of gene expression including those involved in synapse formation, a-Wave neurons once placed in the target region of p-Wave may readily form synapses with the p-Wave targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the segmental homology of a-Wave and p-Wave neurons.

claim: a-Wave neurons once placed in the target region of p-Wave may readily form synapses with the p-Wave targets.
source: Furthermore, since a-Wave and p-Wave neurons are segmental homologs and likely share a large fraction of gene expression including those involved in synapse formation, a-Wave neurons once placed in the target region of p-Wave may readily form synapses with the p-Wave targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the segmental homology and shared gene expression of a-Wave and p-Wave neurons.

claim: There appears to be mechanism(s) that suppress functional connectivity to alternative downstream circuits so that only one behavioral output is induced.
source: Second, there appears to be mechanism(s) that suppress functional connectivity to alternative downstream circuits so that only one behavioral output is induced.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that a-Wave neurons in DFz2 KD animals lose backward-inducing ability despite retaining anterior axon projections.

claim: The ability of a-Wave to induce backward locomotion is greatly reduced in DFz2 KD animals, and instead, forward-inducing ability is conferred.
source: Nonetheless, the ability of a-Wave to induce backward locomotion is greatly reduced, and instead, forward-inducing ability is conferred.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Connectivity from a-Wave axons to backward-inducing circuits is functionally suppressed in DFz2 KD animals, possibly by weakening of functional synapses between the synaptic partners and/or via reciprocal inhibition between the antagonistic downstream circuits.
source: This suggests that connectivity from a-Wave axons to backward-inducing circuits is functionally suppressed, possibly by weakening of functional synapses between the synaptic partners and/or via reciprocal inhibition between the antagonistic downstream circuits.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of backward-inducing ability despite intact anterior axon projections.

claim: Switching in motor commands can be induced by manipulating a single gene in a single class of neurons.
source: The observation that switching in motor commands can be induced by manipulating a single gene in a single class of neurons raises the possibility that the Wave circuitry may be relatively amenable to evolutionary modification (Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998), potentially allowing adaptation to species-specific tactile environments.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the DFz2 KD experiments showing behavioral changes.

claim: The Wave circuitry may be relatively amenable to evolutionary modification, potentially allowing adaptation to species-specific tactile environments.
source: The observation that switching in motor commands can be induced by manipulating a single gene in a single class of neurons raises the possibility that the Wave circuitry may be relatively amenable to evolutionary modification (Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998), potentially allowing adaptation to species-specific tactile environments.
evidence: This is inferred from the ease of rerouting motor commands by manipulating a single gene.

claim: Larval responses to head touch differ among closely related species of Drosophila.
source: Supporting this idea, we observed that larval responses to head touch, where Wave neurons are thought to play major roles, differ among closely related species of Drosophila (S Takagi and AN, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished observations.

claim: There is a degree of flexibility in the command system that might facilitate behavioral evolution.
source: These results point to a degree of flexibility in the command system that might facilitate behavioral evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the ease of rerouting motor commands and the observed species differences in tactile responses.

claim: The present study provides insight into how segment-specific motor commands may be established along the A-P axis during development.

claim: R60G09-GAL4 targets Wave neurons consistently from embryonic to larval stages.
source: We identified in the FlyLight database a sparse GAL4 line, R60G09-GAL4, which targets Wave neurons in 3rd instar larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) with the exception of a single pair of ascending neurons in T2 in the VNC, and also drives expression in two pairs of segmental neurons in the embryo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: One of the GAL4-targeted embryonic neurons is a Wave neuron, which was continuously marked and thus can be traced through embryonic stages to larval stages.
source: Stage-by-stage observation revealed that one of the GAL4-targeted embryonic neurons is a Wave neuron, which was continuously marked and thus can be traced through embryonic stages (10, 12, 16, 18, and 20 hAEL; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B−D) to larval stages (3rd instar; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Another GAL4-targeted non-Wave neuron is dMP2.
source: Another GAL4-targeted non-Wave neurons (that reside posteriorly to Wave with the cell size being larger) started to get fragmented and densely stained in 16 hAEL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and was extinct at later stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E) in segments anterior to A5, suggesting that this neuron is dMP2 (Miguel-Aliaga and Thor, 2004; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the morphology and developmental pattern shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and previous work (Miguel-Aliaga and Thor, 2004; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2008).

claim: The GAL4-driven expression in dMP2 neurons vanished in larval stages.
source: Although dMP2 neurons in segments A6-A8 are known to survive up to larval stages, the GAL4-driven expression in dMP2 neurons vanished in these stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Not all the boutons were Brp+ (co-labeled with Bruchpilot).
source: While not all the boutons were Brp+ (Figure 2A and B), we observed that synapses are formed at all the neuromere where the A4-Wave axon is projecting (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Fast-forward locomotion occurs in the context of escape from nociceptive inputs and is considered a distinct behavior from normal forward locomotion (e.g. during navigation) of the larvae.
source: Fast-forward locomotion occurs in the context of escape from nociceptive inputs and is considered a distinct behavior from normal forward locomotion (e.g. during navigation) of the larvae (Ohyama et al., 2013; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work (Ohyama et al., 2013; Ohyama et al., 2015).

claim: The increased turning in DFz2 KD animals is likely due to the disinhibition of turning-inducing pathways (through other second-order tactile interneurons) by the deterioration of the backward-inducing pathway (through Wave).
source: Since turning is not induced by Wave activation (Takagi et al., 2017), it is likely that the increased turning is due to the disinhibition of turning-inducing pathways (through other second-order tactile interneurons) by the deterioration of the backward-inducing pathway (through Wave).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that turning is not induced by Wave activation and the increased turning in DFz2 KD animals.

claim: The contributions of dendritic alterations to the DFz2 KD phenotypes remain unclear.
source: It should be noted, however, that while the DFz2 KD phenotypes are consistent with aberrant wiring of a-Wave axons to forward locomotion-promoting circuits, the contributions of dendritic alterations remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in the Discussion.
